## Introduction

Today, most of ComEd's residential customers pay a flat rate. That means their
electricity costs them the same price at every hour of the day. But this year,
ComEd is introducing two new time-of-use (TOU) rates. Under TOU rates customers
pay more for energy when the power grid is under strain, and less when demand is
smaller. So electricity is expensive when everyone blasts their AC on a hot
summer afternoon but cheap at 1 AM that same night.

Residential customers who sign up for one of these two programs have an
opportunity to save on their electricity bills. They can pay less for energy by
using it during the cheaper off-peak hours and avoiding the expensive peak
hours. But how much money could they save, exactly? And who would save the most?

This memo analyzes data from smart meters installed across ComEd's service
territory. These devices track how much electricity a customer uses on a
half-hourly basis: making it easy to compare the costs of the same behavior
under different rate structures. Three questions guide the analysis:

1. How would different households' bills change under ComEd's new TOU rates?
2. Would lower-income households be negatively affected?
3. If one of the two new TOU rates outperforms the other, why?

We compare `{python} f"{n_households_jan:,}"` to
`{python} f"{n_households_jul:,}"` accounts across the peak months for heating
(January) and cooling (July) to measure the bill effects of ComEd's Delivery
Time of Use (DTOU) and Rate BEST.

- **More than `{python} f"{pct_save_worst_case:.0f}"`% of households would save money under either TOU rate structure.**
Even in the least favorable scenario (DTOU in July) `{python}
f"{pct_save_dtou_jul:.1f}"`% of households would pay less than they do under the
flat rate, even with no change in behavior. Under Rate BEST in January, that
figure rises to `{python} f"{pct_save_stou_jan:.1f}"`%.

- **Neither rate structure would disproportionately burden lower-income communities.**
We measured savings as the percentage of each household's total bill to account
for the fact that wealthier households have larger bills. Neither DTOU nor Rate

mildly progressive. In other words, during the summer lower-income neighborhoods
save a larger share of their bill than higher-income ones. Under Rate BEST in
July, the lowest-income quintile of neighborhoods would save
 **`{python} f"{stou_jul_q1_pct_savings:.1f}"`%** of their bill, compared to
 **`{python} f"{stou_jul_q5_pct_savings:.1f}"`%** for the highest-income

- **The average block group would save `{python} f"${bg_mean_stou_jan:.2f}"` per month under Rate BEST in January, compared to `{python} f"${bg_mean_dtou_jan:.2f}"` under DTOU** — roughly three to four times more. Across
both seasons, monthly savings range from `{python} f"${bg_mean_dtou_jul:.2f}"`
(DTOU in July) to `{python} f"${bg_mean_stou_jan:.2f}"` (Rate BEST in January).
These savings are driven by Rate BEST's supply charges, which are far below the
current flat supply rate during off-peak hours.

- **Rate BEST's large projected savings depend on illustrative, "placeholder" supply rates that ComEd has not yet finalized.**

which ComEd submitted to the Illinois Commerce Commission (ICC) last year. They
are not binding tariff rates. Rate BEST launches in June 2026, and ComEd has not
announced its actual rates. Both the direction and magnitude of our findings
would depend on the final supply rate levels ComEd sets. The presence and
magnitude of our modeled savings should not be treated as a forecast.


## Background: How electricity bills work

ComEd residential bills have two main components: **supply** and **delivery**. Supply is the cost of generating the electricity itself. Delivery is the cost of the poles and wires that transport that electricity to your home. In other words, you pay for both the energy you use and the cost of getting it to you.

:::{.column-margin}
**Supply** is the wholesale cost of generating power. **Delivery** is the cost of the infrastructure that transports it to your home.
:::

Most ComEd residential customers pay a **flat rate** for their electricity. That means the price of a unit of energy is the same for every hour of the day. Do your laundry at 2pm? You'll pay the same amount as if you did it at 2am. Unfortunately, flat rates don't account for a critical fact: electricity costs more to generate and deliver at some points during the day than others. On a hot summer afternoon, millions of people understandably crank their air conditioners. The grid is under strain, so the cost of meeting customer demand spikes. At 3 AM that same night, demand and the cost of meeting it lowers.

**Time-of-use (TOU) rates** replace that single flat price with prices that vary across different periods of the day. Prices are higher during peak usage hours, lower during off-peak hours. The idea is straightforward: charge more when electricity costs more to provide, and charge less when it doesn't.

Both of ComEd's new TOU programs divide the day into four time blocks: Morning (6 AM–1 PM), Mid-Day Peak (1–7 PM), Evening (7–9 PM), and Overnight (9 PM–6 AM). But the two programs differ in which part of the bill they change from the standard flat rate.

:::{.column-margin}
**DTOU (Delivery Time-of-Use)** varies only the delivery charge by time of day. The supply charge stays flat.
:::

The **Delivery Time-of-Use (DTOU)** program changes only the delivery side of the bill.[^fn-dtou] Supply stays the same as ComEd's flat rate. During the expensive mid-day peak window, the delivery charge rises to roughly 10.7¢ per kilowatt-hour, compared to about 5.9¢ under the flat rate; during overnight hours, it drops by about half. DTOU took effect in January 2026 as a voluntary, opt-in program.

[^fn-dtou]: DTOU was approved in the ICC's Final Order of January 16, 2025 (Docket 24-0378).

:::{.column-margin}
**Rate BEST** is a bundled time-of-use structure that varies both supply and delivery charges by time of day and season.
:::

The **Rate BEST** program goes further.[^fn-rate-best] It varies *both* supply and delivery charges by the time of day. While the delivery side follows the same four time blocks as DTOU, the supply side adds in additional factors. Firstly, Rate BEST's supply side adds seasonal differentiation (summer rates are higher than non-summer rates). What's more, the supply charge obeys the same logic as DTOU's delivery charges: high costs during the peak, low ones in the off peak periods. Rate BEST launches in June 2026 as a voluntary, bundled package: customers who opt in receive both the time-varying supply rate and DTOU delivery together.

[^fn-rate-best]: Rate BEST was approved on rehearing (ICC Order of July 17, 2025, Docket 24-0378).

So what's the difference for your electricity bill? The more parts of your bill that vary by time of day, the more *when* you use electricity (and not just how much) matters. Because demand costs are relatively stable throughout the day, under DTOU timing matters relatively little. But as this memo shows, under Rate BEST, timing could produce big savings for ComEd customers.

## Scope and approach

We simulate what `{python} f"{n_households_jan:,}"` to
`{python} f"{n_households_jul:,}"` ComEd residential accounts would have paid
under each TOU rate structure, using their 2023 half-hour usage data. We then
compare those simulated bills to what each household would have paid under the
current flat rate to measure who saves, who pays more, and whether the answer
differs by income.

The analysis makes the following assumptions:

- **Two months, representing seasonal extremes.** We model January 2023 (peak
heating) and July 2023 (peak cooling). These months capture the periods when
electricity bills are highest and usage patterns diverge the most. Shoulder
months (spring and fall) are not modeled. Annual net impact cannot be determined
from two months alone.

- **2025/2026 rates applied to 2023 usage.** For flat rates, we use the 2026
non-summer and the 2025 summer prices (2026 summer prices have not yet been
released). The new TOU rate schedules are also from 2026. These are applied to
2023 consumption patterns. Our findings are the result of a constructed
simulation: not a report on historical behavior.

- **No behavioral response.** We assume households do not change when or how much
electricity they use in response to TOU pricing. In practice, increased costs
might cause customers to shift usage away from peak hours, which would increase
their savings. Our estimates are conservative and represent a floor on potential
savings rather than a ceiling.

- **Anonymized smart meter data.** ComEd's interval data are released under
ICC-approved privacy rules that strip all customer identifiers (name, address,
account number) and apply an anonymity screen: a customer's data can only be
included if their geographic area contains at least 15 customers in the same
delivery class, and no single customer represents 15% or more of that area's
total load.[^fn-anon] Customers who do not pass this screen are excluded from the
dataset entirely. In practice, ComEd's dense service territory (northern
Illinois, including Chicago) means most customers pass the screen — though
sparsely populated Census block groups are excluded.

[^fn-anon]: The anonymity screen was adopted by the ICC in Docket No. 13-0506
and is commonly known as the 15/15 Rule.

- **No cross-month tracking of individual households.** ComEd regenerates
anonymous account identifiers each month. There is no persistent ID linking a
given household's January record to its July record. We cannot identify which
specific households saved in both months or how individual bill impacts vary
across seasons.

- **Percentage of bill as the equity metric.** To assess whether TOU rates are
regressive or progressive, we measure savings as a percentage of each household's
total flat-rate bill. This controls for the fact that higher-income households
tend to have larger bills (and therefore larger dollar savings) regardless of rate
design. A rate is progressive if lower-income neighborhoods save a larger share
of their bill, and regressive if they save a smaller share.

- **Census block group income as the income proxy.** We use median household
income at the Census block group level (from the American Community Survey 5-year
estimates) as our measure of neighborhood income. Block groups are small
geographic areas of roughly 600–3,000 people. This captures neighborhood-level
patterns but does not identify individual low-income households within
high-income block groups, or vice versa.[^fn-bg-income]

[^fn-bg-income]: Approximately 6.6% of modeled households fall in block groups
without valid Census income data and are excluded from the regression and
quintile analyses. Household-level statistics (e.g., the share of households
that save) use the full account counts.

- **Rate BEST supply rates are illustrative.** The supply charges used for Rate
BEST come from ComEd's Compromise Proposal (ICC Docket 24-0378), not from a
final tariff. These rates have not been finalized.

## Findings

### How would bills change under DTOU?

DTOU is the more modest of the two reforms. Delivery charges are relatively
stable throughout the day compared to supply charges, so the bill impacts are
small in absolute terms. However, they are also widespread.

Under DTOU, the vast majority of households would save money with no change in
behavior. Even in the least favorable scenario (July),
**`{python} f"{pct_save_dtou_jul:.1f}"`%** of households would pay less under
DTOU than under the flat rate. In January, that figure rises to
**`{python} f"{pct_save_dtou_jan:.1f}"`%**. The average block group would save
**$`{python} f"{bg_mean_dtou_jan:.2f}"`** in January and
**$`{python} f"{bg_mean_dtou_jul:.2f}"`** in July.

<!-- TODO: fig-map-dtou-jan — Felt map of mean bill change under DTOU, January.
     Blue = saves, red = pays more. Color range ±$25.45. -->

<!-- TODO: fig-map-dtou-jul — Felt map of mean bill change under DTOU, July. -->

The maps tell a straightforward story. In January, the territory is
predominantly blue — nearly every block group saves money on average. In July,
the pattern is similar but with slightly more variation: a small number of block
groups in Chicago proper shift toward breakeven, reflecting neighborhoods with
flatter usage patterns.

Is the pattern equitable? We measure equity by expressing each household's
savings as a percentage of their total flat-rate bill. This allows us to control
for the fact that wealthier households simply have bigger bills. On this measure,
**DTOU is not meaningfully regressive in either season.** In winter, the income
gradient on percentage savings is trivially small: the lowest-income quintile of
block groups would save **`{python} f"{dtou_jan_q1_pct:.1f}"`%** of their bill,
compared to **`{python} f"{dtou_jan_q5_pct:.1f}"`%** for the highest-income
quintile. This gap of `{python} f"{dtou_jan_q1q5_gap:.1f}"` percentage points
has no practical policy significance.[^fn-dtou-jan-r2]

[^fn-dtou-jan-r2]: The pooled DTOU January regression is statistically significant (p < 0.0001) but has an R² of approximately 1%. Income explains essentially none of the variation in percentage savings.

In summer, the pattern tilts progressive. Lower-income block groups would save a
larger share of their bill than higher-income ones:
**`{python} f"{dtou_jul_q1_pct:.1f}"`%** for the lowest-income quintile versus
**`{python} f"{dtou_jul_q5_pct:.1f}"`%** for the highest — a gap of
`{python} f"{dtou_jul_q1q5_gap:.1f}"` percentage points. In other words, the
modest delivery-only reform slightly favors lower-income neighborhoods in summer
and is essentially neutral in winter.

### How would bills change under Rate BEST?

The results of modeling Rate BEST are far more dramatic. Because it varies both
supply and delivery charges by time of day, the bill impacts are substantially
larger and the equity patterns are sharper.

The savings are near-universal. In January,
**`{python} f"{pct_save_stou_jan:.1f}"`%** of households would save money under
Rate BEST. In July, **`{python} f"{pct_save_stou_jul:.1f}"`%** would save. The
average block group would save **$`{python} f"{bg_mean_stou_jan:.2f}"`** in
January and **$`{python} f"{bg_mean_stou_jul:.2f}"`** in July — roughly three to
four times the DTOU savings.

<!-- TODO: fig-map-stou-jan — Felt map of mean bill change under Rate BEST,
     January. Blue = saves. Color range ±$25.45. -->

The January map is entirely blue. Every single block group saves money on
average. The uniformity is striking, and it's driven by the structure of Rate
BEST's supply rates, which we'll examine in the next section.

<!-- TODO: fig-map-stou-jul — Felt map of mean bill change under Rate BEST,
     July. Color range ±$25.45. -->

The July map shows more texture. Savings are still overwhelmingly positive, but
the variation across neighborhoods is greater. Some block groups, particularly
multi-family areas in central Chicago with flatter load profiles, show smaller
savings. This leads us back to the question of equity.

**In summer, Rate BEST is mildly progressive.** Lower-income block groups would
save a larger share of their bill than higher-income ones. Across all delivery
classes, the lowest-income quintile would save
**`{python} f"{stou_jul_q1_pct_savings:.1f}"`%** of their July bill, compared to
**`{python} f"{stou_jul_q5_pct_savings:.1f}"`%** for the highest-income
quintile: a gap of
**`{python} f"{stou_jul_q1q5_gap:.1f}"` percentage points**.

The scatterplot makes the summer pattern visible. Each dot is a block group. The
downward slope confirms that lower-income neighborhoods save a proportionally
larger share of their bill. The relationship is modest (income explains about
`{python} f"{stou_jul_r2:.1f}"`% of the variation) but it is statistically
robust and consistent across delivery classes. Among single-family gas-heated
homes (C23), the largest customer class, the pattern is monotonic across all five
income quintiles: **`{python} f"{c23_stou_jul_q1_pct:.2f}"`%** for the
lowest-income quintile, declining steadily to
**`{python} f"{c23_stou_jul_q5_pct:.2f}"`%** for the highest — a gap of
**`{python} f"{c23_stou_jul_q1q5_gap:.1f}"` percentage points**.

**In winter, the income gradient on percentage savings disappears.** The pooled
Rate BEST January regression is not statistically significant
(p = `{python} f"{stou_jan_p_value:.3f}"`). Percentage savings hover around
`{python} f"{stou_jan_mean_pct:.1f}"`% across all income quintiles, with no
meaningful trend. In other words, everyone saves roughly the same share of their
bill in winter, regardless of income.

::: {.callout-note}
Higher-income block groups save more in absolute dollars under both rate
structures, in both seasons. This is a bill-size artifact: larger homes consume
more electricity, producing larger bills and larger dollar differences. It is not
evidence of regressivity.
:::


### Why does Rate BEST save so much more?

Rate BEST produces savings three to four times larger than DTOU. Why? The answer
is not about when people use electricity. It's about the level of Rate BEST's
off-peak supply rates.

Under the current flat rate, ComEd customers pay roughly
**`{python} f"{flat_ptc_nonsummer:.3f}"`¢ per kilowatt-hour** for supply (the
Price to Compare). Under the illustrative "placeholder" rates that ComEd showed
the ICC, Rate BEST's Compromise Proposal, the off-peak supply charges (morning,
evening, and overnight) range from roughly
**`{python} f"{bestec_low:.1f}"`¢ to `{python} f"{bestec_high:.1f}"`¢**. That is
a discount of **60–70%** below the flat rate during most hours of the day.

Most residential electricity consumption falls outside the expensive mid-day peak
window (1–7 PM). The math is simple: when off-peak rates are 60–70% below the
flat rate, and most consumption is off-peak, nearly every household saves money.
The mid-day peak supply charge (roughly
`{python} f"{bestec_peak_summer:.1f}"`¢ in summer) is high, but it applies to a
relatively small share of the total consumption. For the vast majority of
households, the big off-peak savings overwhelm the peak penalty.

This is why `{python} f"{pct_save_stou_jan:.1f}"`% of households save under Rate
BEST in January. It is not because those households have unusually favorable
usage patterns. It is because the off-peak supply rates ComEd has provided so far
are so low.

::: {.callout-important}
**The Compromise Proposal rates are illustrative: not final.** The values used in
this simulation were submitted by ComEd as part of stakeholder negotiations (ICC
Docket 24-0378). They are not binding tariff rates. Rate BEST launches in June
2026, and ComEd has not announced its actual supply rates. If the final off-peak
values were set at 7–8¢ per kilowatt-hour instead of 3–4¢, the savings
documented in this memo would shrink dramatically and the equity patterns could
shift.
:::
